comments.author: @D4FChennel
comments.text:
I’ve been spending a lot of time in Vietnam, and honestly, this video doesn’t really match my experience.

Of course scams exist — just like anywhere. I’ve taken taxis, bought things at markets and shops, and sometimes noticed different prices. But I usually check a few places first, get an idea of the normal price, and then decide. Once you know roughly what something should cost, it’s not difficult to avoid being overcharged.

For me, Vietnam feels like a very safe place overall. I’ve spent a lot of time here and have had overwhelmingly normal, friendly interactions with people.

I think there’s a big difference between saying “scams happen in Vietnam” and making it sound like Vietnam is full of scammers. The first is true; the second doesn’t match my experience at all.

comments.author: @ArneRolfsson
comments.text: I just remembered a funny thing that happened to me in Nha Trang. If you've been in Vietnam for a while you've probably encountered the odd motorcycle driver approaching you, asking: How long have you been in Vietnam? If you say anything less than 1-3 months he would try to sell you a guided tour package of his own. But whenever I said I've been here 6 month or more, they just said oh, and drove away. So my advice is never let anyone who approach you know that you're a newbie!

comments.author: @ArneRolfsson
comments.text:
There's so many different scams, here as in many other countries. Personally I've had a very "friendly" Grab driver who in the end planned to dump me in a crocodile farm after robbing me. Buying cigarettes by street vendors around 75% more expensive. Scales at local markets 
weighing 10-15% wrong. Oranges injected with sugar solution. The shoe shine guys, another Grab driver trying to snatch my phone. An old woman trying to sell a banana pancake for 100.000 dong. And so on. It's a never ending story. Yet I've been living here for almost 6 years now and wouldn't want to be anywhere else. Because most people are really friendly and curious and want to interact. Crimes of course do happen but they are solved in a rapid pace. And obviously not all taxi drivers are scammers. I once dropped my phone, essential for me to survive, in a taxi in HCMC. After 10 minutes he returned where he dropped me off with my phone and completely refused the money I wanted to give him.

I don’t agree with what you said about never taking taxis, even metered ones. It really depends on which taxi company you use. VinaSun and Mai Linh are both 100% safe. I’ve been using them for the past 15 years and never had any issues.

You just need to make sure you’re getting into the correct taxi—not all white taxis are VinaSun, and not all green ones are Mai Linh, so double-check before you hop in.

I do use Grab when I’m in the city, but not from the airport because I don’t want to walk across the street and wait in the long line. Taxis are easy to get and don’t cost much more.

comments.author: @CurareDartman
comments.text:
Just arrived in Hanoi yesterday. Three meals out of three and we have been ripped off and treated rudely and with contempt. Mine and my friends' accommodation is expensive and simply unsanitary. Most of the buildings are unfit to live in with mould, large cavities in the floors and walls, broken plumbing and unsafe electrical wiring. It's a dirty town with dogs hit and garbage strewn about the streets, dirty gutters and hygiene in food outlets is poor. I was planning to stay three weeks, but I'm flying back to Thailand tomorrow. I was here 20 years ago and nothing has changed. One of my friends and I both ran separate successful restaurants in Australia for decades so we know all about hospitality. Sadly, Hanoi is not welcoming, nor accommodating towards tourists. The people here want to make a quick buck from minimal work and no respect for the customer. Keep your Viet Nam and I'll continue to enjoy the wonderful hospitality of the good people of Thailand. 
There's a reason why only 10% of tourists return to Vietnam.

comments.text:
Scam 5 is pretty common. I visited Vietnam recently and both in Hanoi and Saigon they tried this on me. I let it go because it was not a significant amount, but going forward I will simply ignore the aunties. 

1) Aunty walked towards me and offered me a free pastry ball (tasted actually pretty good, it was dry and old, but it was good). I asked how much. She said 30k, so I said yes, gave her 200k and she did not return enough change and said (after I asked) the price was 80k for 5 of the pastry balls, which obviously is overpriced. Clearly, she lied. As it turned out, she only returned 110k effectively charging 90k. In any case, I let it go. It was my first evening in Hanoi and I did not want to get upset.

2) Bought some fruit and similarly to 1) after I paid 100k for fruit that was supposed to cost 85k, I only received 5k with the aunty then saying the total was 95k. Again, too small of an amount to bother. The fruit was actually pretty good (in particular the bananas). 

In any case, I will have pen and paper with me and will be exceedingly careful if at all I ever buy from street aunties in Vietnam. And I will carry small denomination bills so that I can pay exactly what was agreed upon after taking possession of the products first. But, to be honest, to the most part I will not bother and ignore those cute aunties. Love Vietnam, but this reflects poorly on the country.
